title: Corporate social responsibility

definition.text: Companies running their main business responsibly and sustainably so that their overall effect on society is positive.

facts.text: It is a form of private business self-regulation that aims to help social and environmental goals by reducing harm, such as cutting a firm's carbon footprint.
Since the 1960s it has gone by many names, including corporate sustainability, sustainable business, corporate citizenship and responsible business, and there is little agreement on a definition.
A business person may see it as strategy, an NGO activist as greenwash and a government official as voluntary regulation.
Howard Bowen's 1953 book Social Responsibilities of the Businessman is widely seen as the founding work; he argued business leaders' duties go beyond making profit.
Firms take it up for strategic, ethical or instrumental reasons; for listed companies it often takes the form of ESG practices and reports.
It has been shifting from voluntary choices by single firms toward mandatory schemes at regional, national and international levels.
Its scope widened from a firm's own conduct to its suppliers, how its products are used and how they are thrown away.
Supporters say it raises long-term profits; critics say it distracts from a firm's economic role or is mere window-dressing.

contested_note: Supporters argue CSR raises long-term profits, while critics say it distracts from business's economic role or is window-dressing.

title: Stakeholder theory

definition.text: The view that a firm is answerable not only to its shareholders but to every group with a relationship to it, such as workers, customers, suppliers and communities.

facts.text: The word stakeholder was coined in English by Eric Rhenman in his 1968 book Industrial Democracy and Industrial Management; R. Edward Freeman later developed the theory.
A review of 14,523 articles found the stakeholder view to be the most common dimension of CSR.
One reason firms adopt CSR is to satisfy stakeholders beyond their shareholders.
The EU defines CSR as a firm being accountable for its impact on all relevant stakeholders.
Critics say the stakeholder view ignores how complex the networks in cross-sector partnerships are.

notes: No crawled page of its own; passes test 5 (stakeholders discussed on Corporate social responsibility, Corporate environmental responsibility and Sustainable business). Suggested page: Stakeholder theory.

definition.text: Archie Carroll's four-part framework of what society expects of business: economic, legal, ethical and philanthropic responsibilities.

facts.text: Carroll began developing it after his 1979 Academy of Management Review article on corporate social performance.
It is often drawn as a pyramid of responsibilities: economic, legal, ethical and philanthropic.

title: Shareholder value versus social responsibility

definition.text: The argument over whether a company exists only to earn returns for its owners within the law, or also owes duties to society and the environment.

facts.text: Milton Friedman argued a firm's purpose is to maximize returns to shareholders, and that obeying the law is socially responsible enough.
Friedman said people may spend their own money on causes, but owners should not raise prices to fund social goals unrelated to profit, which he likened to a tax on consumers.
In the 1930s Berle and Dodd debated whether directors should be bound by enforceable rules to serve labour, customers and the public as well as shareholders.
Some argue better government regulation is the alternative to voluntary CSR; others reply that mandated programs distort how resources are allocated.
Some studies find CSR serves managers' interests at shareholders' cost, a kind of agency problem.

contested_note: Friedman and others hold that a firm's only duty is profit within the law, while CSR supporters argue firms owe wider duties to society.

title: Social license to operate
article: Corporate social responsibility#Social license to operate

definition.text: The ongoing support and approval that local communities and other stakeholders give to a company's activities.

facts.text: The term was introduced in 1997 and has been used mostly in resource extraction industries to describe company-community relations.
Without it, local people may block projects, staff may leave and firms may face ongoing legal challenges.
It is granted by communities, not governments, and can take a long time to win but be lost very quickly.
It rests on relationships and trust; local firms tend to gain it more easily than outside ones.
Showing commitment to CSR is one way to earn it, by improving a firm's reputation.

definition.text: Six kinds of activity through which companies practise CSR, from donations to behaviour-change campaigns.

facts.text: They are corporate philanthropy, community volunteering, socially responsible business practices, cause promotion, cause-related marketing and corporate social marketing.
Philanthropy and volunteering usually have no profit motive; the rest can be cause marketing, which pursues both profit and social good.

title: Social accounting
article: Corporate social responsibility#Accounting, auditing, and reporting

definition.text: Reporting the social and environmental effects of a company's economic activity to interest groups and to society at large.

facts.text: It stresses that corporations should be accountable for their effects.
There is no single fixed standard; frameworks include AA1000, based on the triple bottom line, the Global Reporting Initiative guidelines and ISO 14000.

title: Socially responsible investing

definition.text: Investors using where they put their money to encourage company behaviour they consider responsible.

facts.text: What counts as ethical varies: some religious investors withdraw money from firms that offend their views, while secular investors divest from firms imposing religious views.

notes: May duplicate an investing entry in the finance-for-conservation chapter.

title: CSR as misdirection

definition.text: The criticism that companies use social responsibility programs to draw attention away from harmful parts of their business.

facts.text: Unproven social claims and outright greenwashing have made consumers more cynical and distrustful.
The tobacco industry funded research in genetics, viruses and air pollution, which drew attention from the link between smoking and cancer.
US firms convicted of bribery got more lenient fines if they were seen to engage in CSR: a 20% rise in corporate giving went with a 40% lower fine.
A review of 700 sources found firms engage in CSR mainly for expected financial gain rather than a wish to serve society.

contested_note: Critics see CSR as a distraction from harmful practices, while supporters see it as genuine responsibility.

title: Resource-based view of CSR

definition.text: A way of judging the costs and benefits of CSR by asking whether it gives a firm a competitive advantage that rivals cannot copy.

facts.text: Barney (1990) held that lasting advantage needs resources that are valuable, rare, inimitable and non-substitutable.
Reinhardt (1998) found a CSR-based strategy earns above-normal returns only if competitors cannot imitate it.
McWilliams and Siegel argued managers can set CSR spending through cost-benefit analysis like any other investment.
Waddock and Graves (1997) linked social and financial performance; McWilliams and Siegel (2000) said innovation, not CSR, drove the gains.

contested_note: Researchers disagree on whether CSR itself or innovation explains the link between social and financial performance.

definition.text: Choosing what to buy, and what to boycott, according to how products affect people, animals and the environment.

facts.text: It is a form of consumer activism based on 'dollar voting'.
Its rise over the last two decades is linked to the rise of CSR.
Criteria-based ethical and environmental ratings of companies, first used for shoppers, are now common in business sustainability ratings, and ESG ratings reach stock traders' screens.
More consumers demand sustainable goods, especially when they think firms neglect the environment.
Its growth is held back by routine buying that leaves no room for reflection and by competing moral demands in daily life.

definition.text: The gap between consumers saying they will buy only from responsible companies and what they actually buy.

facts.text: Many consumers want to buy from responsible firms, yet ethical purchases are a small share of household spending.
One explanation is the bystander effect: people act less when others seem not to care.
Another is that ethical products cost more but give the buyer little extra in return.
A Lisbon study found price, limited access and lack of education held back less engaged shoppers of sustainable fashion.

title: Nature-positive

definition.text: A goal to halt and reverse the loss of nature by 2030 and to achieve its full recovery by 2050.

facts.text: Progress is measured against a baseline of biodiversity in 2020.
It matches the 2030 mission and 2050 vision of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, though the framework does not name it.
It was proposed as a single global goal for nature to sit beside climate and development goals, aiming at an 'Equitable, Nature-Positive, Carbon Neutral world'.
Unlike earlier approaches, it covers a company's whole value chain, not just direct impacts, and aims for absolute rather than relative gains.
Over 90 world leaders signed the Leaders' Pledge for Nature, and the G7 committed to it at its 2021 summit.
Critics call it vague and open to greenwashing, and warn of the 'financialization of nature'.
To avoid greenwashing, Milner-Gulland proposed it needs a measured baseline, timeframe, target, clear actions, regular monitoring and disclosure.
Its 'net' approach is criticised for implying continued loss and assuming like-for-like compensation is possible.

contested_note: Critics call nature-positive vague, open to greenwashing and a route to financializing nature, while its proponents say business must be part of the solution.

definition.text: A goal for a project whose harm to biodiversity is outweighed by steps to reduce, repair and offset that harm.

facts.text: No net loss aims to cancel out biodiversity loss, while net positive impact aims for a net gain.
Both usually apply the mitigation hierarchy (avoid, minimise, rehabilitate, restore, offset) to an organisation's direct impacts, which are only a small part of its total effect.
Their ambition has been set at project level against a declining baseline, not against overall targets.

title: Mainstreaming nature in business

definition.text: Building nature into a company's decision-making, governance, strategy and risk management rather than leaving it to site ecologists.

facts.text: It sets the nature-positive approach apart from no net loss and net positive impact, where biodiversity is handled by ecological managers at project sites.
Since the Kunming-Montreal framework began, nature-positive has helped mainstream nature through businesses and governance systems.

notes: No page of its own; passes test 5 (Nature-positive and Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework). May duplicate a biodiversity mainstreaming entry elsewhere.
